title: When Is Monetary Policy Transmission Strongest? - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed researchers find that Fed policy surprises pass through to longer-horizon Treasury forward rates mainly when inflation is demand-driven (a 1pp near-term shock lifts two-year forwards ~2pp vs ~0.5pp in supply-driven regimes). The mechanism is signaling: forecasters revise their view of the Fed's reaction function only in demand-led episodes, so with supply pressures back, Fed surprises should move long yields less.

themes.theme: Fed reacts asymmetrically to inflation source

insights.claim: Research by Hoffman, Manea and Mojon (2024) finds the Federal Reserve's policy-rate response to demand-driven inflation contributions is about four times larger than its response to supply-driven contributions.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Decompose inflation prints into supply vs demand before forecasting Fed hikes; supply-led inflation draws far less tightening.
insights.quote: the Fed’s response to demand-driven inflation contributions tends to be four times larger than its response to supply-driven contributions
insights.locator: Recent work by Hoffman et al. (2024)

insights.claim: Kakhbod, Kermani and Maciel (2026), analyzing FOMC transcripts and statements, find the Fed's policy path is more sensitive to discussions of demand pressures than supply pressures, attributed to the Fed being more constrained against supply-driven inflation.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: FOMC language emphasizing demand pressures is a stronger hawkish signal than language about supply pressures.
insights.locator: A similar result was found by Kakhbod et al. (2026)

insights.claim: The Fed's weaker response to supply-driven inflation is consistent with the 'balanced approach' in its 2025 Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, which applies when employment and price-stability goals conflict, as they tend to under supply shocks.

insights.claim: Over 2004–2026, a 1 percentage point rise in the demand-driven PCE inflation component is associated with a 0.4 percentage point increase in the effective federal funds rate, while the same rise in the supply-driven component is associated with no change.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: A simple rule of thumb: only demand-driven PCE inflation moves the funds rate (~0.4pp per 1pp).

insights.claim: The San Francisco Fed's Supply- and Demand-Driven PCE Inflation series (Shapiro 2026) classifies category-level price changes as demand-driven when prices and quantities move in the same direction and supply-driven when they move in opposite directions, with an ambiguous residual component.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: This publicly available series is a ready tool for classifying the current inflation regime and its likely policy/market response.

insights.claim: In the Shapiro supply/demand decomposition since 2004, the supply component of PCE inflation tends to move with food and energy prices, while the demand component fluctuates more during recessions.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Energy/food price spikes typically signal supply-driven inflation that the Fed and bond markets respond to less forcefully.

insights.claim: Supply-driven inflation pressures have reemerged since the pandemic, prompting closer examination of how the source of inflation shapes monetary policy.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: A supply-heavy inflation mix is the current regime, which conditions how much rates react to Fed actions.

insights.claim: Treasury instantaneous forward rates show the same pattern as the policy rate: they rise more with demand-driven than supply-driven PCE inflation, though the magnitudes decline as the forward horizon lengthens.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Front-to-intermediate forwards are most exposed to demand-driven inflation surprises; long forwards less so.
insights.quote: Our findings indicate that a similar relationship holds with the forward rates, but the magnitudes decline as the horizon increases.

insights.claim: Financial market participants anticipate a stronger, more persistent Fed response to demand-related inflation pressures than to supply-driven price pressures, and price this into longer-term interest rates.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Bond investors should expect yield curves to reprice more aggressively on demand-led inflation data than on supply-led data.

insights.claim: Level relationships between inflation components and long forward rates may not reflect anticipated policy alone, since longer-term rates also move with term premiums and structural factors such as productivity growth.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Separate expected-policy effects from term-premium moves before attributing long-yield changes to the Fed.

insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Monetary policy transmission to bonds is regime-dependent; size duration bets on Fed surprises by the inflation mix.
insights.quote: Monetary policy surprises primarily feed through to longer-horizon rates when demand-driven inflation is high.

insights.claim: Because supply-side inflation pressures have increased in recent years, monetary policy surprises are likely to have a smaller, more muted impact on longer-horizon yields going forward.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: In the current supply-heavy regime, expect smaller long-end reactions to Fed surprises; the policy rate gets less traction on financial conditions.

insights.claim: Monetary policy transmission to bond markets is strongest during demand-driven inflationary episodes, implying the Fed's ability to tighten financial conditions via long rates is weakest when inflation is supply-driven.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Supply-driven inflation weakens the policy lever on long rates; a key consideration for curve and duration positioning.

insights.claim: Market-based inflation expectations correlate about equally with demand- and supply-driven inflation, suggesting markets expect both kinds of shocks to be similarly persistent, which rules out perceived persistence as the reason for stronger demand-regime transmission.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Don't assume markets see supply shocks as transitory; the transmission gap comes from Fed-reaction signaling instead.

insights.claim: Using the Bauer, Pflueger and Sunderam (2024) series on forecasters' perceived Fed reaction to inflation, professional forecasters do not change their perception during supply-driven imbalances but revise toward a more aggressive Fed response during demand-driven imbalances.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Track perceived Fed reaction-function measures; they shift only in demand-led regimes.

insights.claim: A monetary policy surprise during demand-driven imbalances is read by markets as a signal that the Fed is shifting to a persistently stricter stance, whereas during supply-driven imbalances it may be treated as a one-off.
insights.speaker: Rami Najjar
insights.so_what: Hawkish surprises in demand-led inflation regimes warrant pricing a persistent policy path shift, not a single move.
insights.quote: a monetary policy surprise during demand imbalances serves as a signal that the Fed is shifting to a persistently stricter monetary policy stance
